catalog_quote: [Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002:34-35, Ua Pou] In Marquesan two types of stress are heard, word stress and phrase stress. Word stress is predictable as is phrase stress when it is not being used for emphasis purposes. ... Within such phonological words, stress occurs on the last long vowel, or, in three-syllable words, on the first long vowel, or, if there is no long vowel, on the last diphthong, or, if there is no diphthong, on the penultimate syllable of the word. All single short-syllable words are, as this rule predicts, unstressed. ... Stress placement does not change before final or non-final juncture. ... [m'AtA] 'eye' [hEt'U:] 'star' [pE?'AU] 'speak' ... [veh'ine] 'woman' ... [kAnAh'Au] 'beautiful' [m'a:mA-i] 'egg' ... [p'a:ko:ko:] 'knock (at door)' Further work needs to be carried out to check stress patterns for three-syllable words of different shapes and for the comparatively rare …

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation, the examples, and the fn.22/fn.25 hedges are verbatim in the full text we hold of Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002 at the stated sections/pages, and the Lynch 2002 p.866 secondary quote is verbatim in the held excerpt. Deciding source: a 2002 Pacific Linguistics monograph with a dedicated, first-hand stress section for a lect the authors themselves place in the northern dialect area; it is open access and held in full. The weight-sensitive (tentative) coding faithfully mirrors the source's own hedges (p.35 'Further work needs to be carried out', fn.25 acoustic correlates and secondary stress open, analyst vs native-speaker disagreement in fn.22) and the Mutu vs Lynch/Zewen divergence, so no reclassification is indicated. sources.note: Per Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002:31-32 and fn.19 it analyses the earlier accounts (Elbert, Raapoto 1994, Teikiehuupoko n.d., Dumond Fillon 1992) and argues they conflate word stress with phrase-penultimate vowel extension, a suprasegmental length feature tied to final/non-final juncture (falling vs rising/steady pitch contours); a prosody paper on a Polynesian language, no lexical tone claim expected.

sources.note: Per Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002:31-32: a native-speaker account of word accent and phrase accent; says the long (penultimate) vowel gives Marquesan its rhythm and 'music', treats vowel lengthening as a characteristic of stress, and states that in each sense group stress falls on the main word with a demarcative final lengthening (n.d.a:1, 6); accent description, no tone analysis expected.
